OpenMM is a high-performance, extensible toolkit for molecular simulation. This page introduces the overall architecture, purpose, and key components of the OpenMM codebase, focusing on how different parts interact to provide a flexible and efficient framework for molecular dynamics simulations.

For information about building and installing OpenMM, see [Installation and Getting Started](#1.1). For details on development workflow, see [Development Workflow](#1.2).

## Purpose and Scope

OpenMM serves as both a software library that can be integrated into other applications and as a complete application for running molecular simulations. It provides:

1. A flexible, object-oriented API for setting up and running simulations
2. Multiple high-performance implementations targeting different hardware platforms
3. Extensibility through plugins for specialized force fields and algorithms
4. Support for a wide range of simulation techniques and force fields

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:1-10]()

## System Architecture

### Core Components

OpenMM's architecture is designed around a clean separation between the simulation API and the implementation details for different hardware platforms.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Core API"
        System["System"] --- Forces["Force Classes"]
        System --- Context["Context"]
        Forces --- Context
        Integrator["Integrator Classes"] --- Context
        Platform["Platform"] --- Context
        State["State"] --- Context
    end
    
    subgraph "Platform Implementations"
        Platform --> Reference["Reference Platform"]
        Platform --> CPU["CPU Platform"]
        Platform --> OpenCL["OpenCL Platform"]
        Platform --> CUDA["CUDA Platform"]
        Platform --> HIP["HIP Platform"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Plugins"
        Forces --> Amoeba["Amoeba Force"]
        Forces --> Drude["Drude Force"]
        Forces --> RPMD["RPMD"]
        Forces --> PME["PME Force"]
    end
```

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:92-95](), [CMakeLists.txt:377-408]()

### Key Classes and Their Roles

- **System**: Defines the physical system being simulated, including particles, constraints, and forces
- **Force**: Represents a specific type of interaction between particles
- **Integrator**: Implements algorithms for advancing the simulation through time
- **Context**: Manages the state of a simulation and coordinates the interaction between System, Force, and Integrator
- **Platform**: Provides hardware-specific implementations of computational kernels
- **State**: Represents the complete state of a simulation at a point in time

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:198-206]()

## Platforms and Kernels

OpenMM achieves performance portability through a platform abstraction that allows the same simulation to run on different hardware.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Platform {
        +getName()
        +createKernel(name, context)
        +registerPlatform()
    }
    
    class KernelImpl {
        <<abstract>>
    }
    
    class KernelFactory {
        +createKernelImpl(name, platform, context)
    }
    
    class CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel {
        +execute()
    }
    
    class UpdateStateDataKernel {
        +getPositions()
        +setPositions()
    }
    
    class ApplyConstraintsKernel {
        +apply()
    }
    
    Platform -- KernelFactory
    KernelFactory -- KernelImpl
    KernelImpl <|-- CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel
    KernelImpl <|-- UpdateStateDataKernel
    KernelImpl <|-- ApplyConstraintsKernel
    
    class ReferenceKernels
    class CPUKernels
    class OpenCLKernels
    class CUDAKernels
    class HIPKernels
    
    CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel <|-- ReferenceKernels
    CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel <|-- CPUKernels
    CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel <|-- OpenCLKernels
    CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel <|-- CUDAKernels
    CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel <|-- HIPKernels
```

OpenMM supports the following hardware platforms:

| Platform | Description | Configuration Option |
|----------|-------------|---------------------|
| Reference | Pure C++ implementation (slow but precise) | Always built |
| CPU | Multi-threaded CPU implementation | `OPENMM_BUILD_CPU_LIB` |
| CUDA | NVIDIA GPU implementation | `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB` |
| OpenCL | Cross-platform GPU implementation | `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB` |
| HIP | AMD GPU implementation | `OPENMM_BUILD_HIP_LIB` |

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:319-357](), [CMakeLists.txt:369-372]()

## Plugin System

OpenMM uses a plugin architecture to allow specialized force fields and algorithms to be added without modifying the core library.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Core OpenMM"
        OpenMM["OpenMM Library"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Force Field Plugins"
        OpenMM --- AmoebaPlugin["OpenMMAmoeba\n(Polarizable FF)"]
        OpenMM --- DrudePlugin["OpenMMDrude\n(Drude Oscillator Model)"]
        OpenMM --- RPMDPlugin["OpenMMRPMD\n(Ring Polymer MD)"]
        OpenMM --- PMEPlugin["OpenMMPME\n(CPU PME)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Platform-Specific Implementations"
        AmoebaPlugin --- AmoebaReference["Amoeba Reference"]
        AmoebaPlugin --- AmoebaCUDA["Amoeba CUDA"]
        AmoebaPlugin --- AmoebaOpenCL["Amoeba OpenCL"]
        
        DrudePlugin --- DrudeReference["Drude Reference"]
        DrudePlugin --- DrudeCUDA["Drude CUDA"]
        DrudePlugin --- DrudeOpenCL["Drude OpenCL"]
        
        RPMDPlugin --- RPMDReference["RPMD Reference"]
        RPMDPlugin --- RPMDCUDA["RPMD CUDA"]
        RPMDPlugin --- RPMDOpenCL["RPMD OpenCL"]
    end
```

Each plugin:
- Implements specialized force types and algorithms
- Provides optimized implementations for different platforms
- Can be enabled/disabled at build time
- Integrates with the core API through standard interfaces

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:376-408](), [plugins/amoeba/CMakeLists.txt:1-13](), [plugins/drude/CMakeLists.txt:1-13](), [plugins/rpmd/CMakeLists.txt:1-13]()

## Python API and Application Layer

OpenMM provides a comprehensive Python API for setting up and running simulations at a higher level than the C++ API.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "C++ Core API"
        CoreAPI["OpenMM C++ API"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Python API"
        CoreAPI --> LowLevelAPI["Low-level Python API"]
        LowLevelAPI --> ForceField["ForceField"]
        LowLevelAPI --> Modeller["Modeller"]
        LowLevelAPI --> Simulation["Simulation"]
        
        subgraph "File I/O"
            LowLevelAPI --> PDBFile["PDBFile"]
            LowLevelAPI --> AmberFile["AmberPrmtopFile"]
            LowLevelAPI --> CharmmFile["CharmmPsfFile"]
            LowLevelAPI --> GromacsFile["GromacsTopFile"]
        end
    end
    
    subgraph "User Code"
        Simulation --> UserSimulation["User Simulation Script"]
        ForceField --> UserSimulation
        FileIO --> UserSimulation
    end
```

A typical Python simulation workflow looks like:

1. Load molecule and topology (PDB, AMBER, CHARMM, GROMACS)
2. Define force field
3. Create System with force field parameters
4. Set up Integrator
5. Create Simulation object combining topology, system, and integrator
6. Run simulation and collect data

Example:
```python
from openmm.app import *
from openmm import *
from openmm.unit import *

pdb = PDBFile('input.pdb')
forcefield = ForceField('amber14-all.xml', 'amber14/tip3pfb.xml')
system = forcefield.createSystem(pdb.topology, nonbondedMethod=PME)
integrator = LangevinMiddleIntegrator(300*kelvin, 1/picosecond, 0.004*picoseconds)
simulation = Simulation(pdb.topology, system, integrator)
simulation.context.setPositions(pdb.positions)
simulation.minimizeEnergy()
simulation.step(10000)
```

Sources: [examples/simulatePdb.py:1-16](), [examples/simulateAmber.py:1-16](), [examples/simulateCharmm.py:1-34](), [examples/simulateGromacs.py:1-16]()

## Versioning and Compatibility

The current major version of OpenMM is 8.2.0, as defined in the build system:

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:157-159]()

## Documentation Structure

The OpenMM documentation is organized into three main parts:

1. **The Application Layer** - Higher-level Python interface for building and running simulations
2. **The Library Layer** - C++ API and direct library usage
3. **The Theory Behind OpenMM** - Algorithms and methods implemented in the library

Sources: [docs-source/usersguide/application.rst:1-19](), [docs-source/usersguide/library.rst:1-22](), [docs-source/usersguide/theory.rst:1-16]()

This wiki provides complementary developer-focused documentation to help understand, modify, and extend the codebase.

This page provides instructions for building, installing, and getting started with OpenMM from source code. If you're looking for information about using the pre-built Python packages, see [The OpenMM Application Layer](#6) or [Python API](#6.1).

## Prerequisites

Before building OpenMM, ensure you have the following dependencies installed:

### Required Dependencies

- **CMake** (version 3.17 or later) - Build system generator
- **C++ compiler** supporting C++11 standard:
  - GCC (Linux)
  - Clang (macOS/Linux) 
  - Visual Studio 2019 or later (Windows)
- **Doxygen** - For generating API documentation from C++ headers

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:24](), [CMakeLists.txt:97]()

### Optional Dependencies for Python Wrappers

- **Python** (3.6 or later) - Required for Python API
- **SWIG** (version 3.0.7 or later) - Interface generator for Python bindings
- **Cython** - For optimized Python extensions
- **NumPy** - For array operations in Python
- **pytest** - For running Python test suite

Sources: [.travis.yml:167-189](), [appveyor.yml:12-14]()

### Optional Dependencies for GPU Platforms

- **CUDA Toolkit** (7.5 or later) - For NVIDIA GPU support via CUDA platform
  - Includes: `nvcc`, `cudart`, CUDA libraries
- **OpenCL** development files - For cross-platform GPU support
  - Includes: OpenCL headers and ICD loader
- **ROCm/HIP** - For AMD GPU support via HIP platform

Sources: [.travis.yml:191-203](), [appveyor.yml:25-41](), [CMakeLists.txt:324-357]()

### Optional Dependencies for Specific Features

- **FFTW3** - For CPU-based PME calculations
- **Gromacs** - For testing Gromacs file format support

Sources: [.travis.yml:9](), [.travis.yml:176]()

## Obtaining the Source Code

Clone the OpenMM repository:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/openmm/openmm.git
cd openmm
```

## Building from Source

OpenMM uses CMake to generate platform-specific build files. Here's the basic build process:

### Build Process Overview

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["Clone Repository"] --> B["Create Build Directory"]
    B --> C["Configure with CMake"]
    C --> D["Build"]
    D --> E["Install"]
    E --> F["Run Tests"]
```

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:14-54](), [CMakeLists.txt:130-150]()

### Detailed Steps

1. **Create a build directory:**
   ```bash
   mkdir build
   cd build
   ```

2. **Configure with CMake:**
   ```bash
   cmake ..
   ```
   
3. **Build OpenMM:**
   ```bash
   make
   ```
   
4. **Install OpenMM:**
   ```bash
   make install
   ```
   
5. **Test the installation:**
   ```bash
   make test
   ```

### Important CMake Configuration Options

The following table shows key CMake options that control which features are built:

#### Core Library Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `OPENMM_BUILD_SHARED_LIB` | ON | Build `libOpenMM.so`/`OpenMM.dll` shared library |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_STATIC_LIB` | OFF | Build `libOpenMM_static.a`/`OpenMM_static.lib` static library |
| `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE` | Release | Build type: Release, Debug, RelWithDebInfo |
| `CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` | `/usr/local/openmm` | Installation directory |

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:72-73](), [CMakeLists.txt:86-88](), [CMakeLists.txt:134-136]()

#### Wrapper and Documentation Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `OPENMM_BUILD_C_AND_FORTRAN_WRAPPERS` | ON | Generate C/Fortran API wrappers using SWIG |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_PYTHON_WRAPPERS` | ON | Generate Python wrappers (requires AMOEBA, RPMD, Drude plugins) |
| `OPENMM_GENERATE_API_DOCS` | OFF | Generate API documentation using Doxygen and Sphinx |
| `BUILD_TESTING` | ON | Build test executables |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_EXAMPLES` | ON | Build example programs |

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:253](), [CMakeLists.txt:437](), [CMakeLists.txt:455](), [CMakeLists.txt:471](), [.travis.yml:94]()

#### Platform-Specific Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `OPENMM_BUILD_REFERENCE_TESTS` | TRUE | Build test cases for Reference platform |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CPU_LIB` | ON | Build optimized CPU platform with SSE/AVX |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB` | Auto† | Build CUDA platform (`libOpenMMCuda.so`) |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB` | Auto† | Build OpenCL platform (`libOpenMMOpenCL.so`) |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_HIP_LIB` | Auto† | Build HIP platform for AMD GPUs (`libOpenMMHIP.so`) |

† Auto-detected based on whether SDK is found by CMake `FIND_PACKAGE` commands.

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:316](), [CMakeLists.txt:369](), [CMakeLists.txt:324-333](), [CMakeLists.txt:336-344](), [CMakeLists.txt:347-357]()

#### Plugin Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `OPENMM_BUILD_AMOEBA_PLUGIN` | ON | Build AMOEBA polarizable force field plugin |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_RPMD_PLUGIN` | ON | Build Ring Polymer MD plugin |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_DRUDE_PLUGIN` | ON | Build Drude oscillator plugin |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_PME_PLUGIN` | ON | Build CPU PME plugin (requires FFTW3) |

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:376](), [CMakeLists.txt:385](), [CMakeLists.txt:394](), [CMakeLists.txt:403]()

#### Testing Options

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `OPENMM_BUILD_SERIALIZATION_TESTS` | TRUE | Build serialization test cases |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CPU_TESTS` | TRUE | Build CPU platform test cases |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_TESTS` | OFF | Build CUDA platform test cases |
| `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_TESTS` | OFF | Build OpenCL platform test cases |

Sources: [serialization/CMakeLists.txt:9](), [platforms/cpu/CMakeLists.txt:15](), [.travis.yml:50-51]()

### Example CMake Configuration

To build with CUDA and OpenCL support:

```bash
cmake .. -DOPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB=ON -DOPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB=ON
```

To build with only CPU support:

```bash
cmake .. -DOPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB=OFF -DOPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB=OFF -DOPENMM_BUILD_CPU_LIB=ON
```

## Platform-Specific Build Instructions

### Linux

**Default Installation Path:** `/usr/local/openmm`

**Compiler Setup:**
```bash
# Set compilers (optional, uses system default otherwise)
export CC=gcc
export CXX=g++
```

**Build Commands:**
```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
make -j2 install
```

**Post-Installation:**
```bash
# Add library path
export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$LD_LIBRARY_PATH:/usr/local/openmm/lib

# For Python wrappers
make PythonInstall
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

**Linux-Specific Considerations:**
- The `-lrt` and `-ldl` libraries are linked automatically on Linux (not Android)
- On ARM and PPC architectures, a newer CMake (3.17.0+) is required

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:62-64](), [CMakeLists.txt:263-267](), [.travis.yml:209-217](), [.travis.yml:138-153]()

### macOS

**Default Installation Path:** `/usr/local/openmm`

**Minimum Deployment Target:** macOS 10.7

**Compiler Setup:**
```bash
# macOS uses clang by default
# Install Homebrew dependencies
brew install fftw doxygen swig
```

**CMake Configuration:**
```bash
mkdir build && cd build
cmake .. \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_DEPLOYMENT_TARGET=10.7 \
  -DCMAKE_OSX_ARCHITECTURES=arm64 \
  -DCMAKE_INSTALL_NAME_DIR="@rpath" \
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release
make -j2 install
```

**Post-Installation:**
```bash
# For Python wrappers
sudo make PythonInstall
python -m openmm.testInstallation
```

**macOS-Specific Considerations:**
- Builds use `libc++` standard library by default
- On x86_64, SSE2 is enabled via `-msse2` flag
- Uses `@rpath` for library install names to improve linking

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:99-121](), [.travis.yml:128-137](), [.travis.yml:210-217]()

### Windows

**Default Installation Path:** `C:\Program Files\OpenMM`

**Visual Studio Setup:**
1. Open "Developer Command Prompt for VS 2019"
2. Set environment for x64:
   ```cmd
   call "C:\Program Files (x86)\Microsoft Visual Studio\2019\Community\VC\Auxiliary\Build\vcvarsall.bat" amd64
   ```

**CMake Configuration:**
```cmd
mkdir build
cd build
cmake .. -G "NMake Makefiles" ^
  -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release ^
  -DOPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB=ON ^
  -DOPENCL_INCLUDE_DIR=C:/opencl/inc ^
  -DOPENCL_LIBRARY=C:/opencl/lib/OpenCL.lib
```

**Build Commands:**
```cmd
cmake --build . --target install
cmake --build . --target PythonInstall
```

**Windows-Specific Considerations:**
- Use `/MD` for release builds (multithreaded DLL runtime)
- Warning levels adjusted: `/W2` instead of default `/W4`
- Warnings 4305 (truncation) and 4244 (conversion) are suppressed
- No special link flags required (unlike Linux `-lrt`)

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:57-65](), [CMakeLists.txt:122-127](), [CMakeLists.txt:268-270](), [appveyor.yml:1-62]()

## OpenMM Architecture Overview

The following diagram shows the main components of OpenMM:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "OpenMM Core Components"
        System["System"]
        Force["Force Classes"]
        Integrator["Integrator Classes"]
        Context["Context"]
        Platform["Platform"]
        State["State"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Platform Implementations"
        Platform --> Reference["Reference Platform"]
        Platform --> CPU["CPU Platform"]
        Platform --> OpenCL["OpenCL Platform"]
        Platform --> CUDA["CUDA Platform"]
        Platform --> HIP["HIP Platform"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Force Plugins"
        Force --> AmoebaForce["Amoeba Force"]
        Force --> DrudeForce["Drude Force"]
        Force --> RPMDForce["RPMD Force"]
        Force --> PMEForce["PME Force"]
    end
    
    Context --- System
    Context --- Force
    Context --- Integrator
    Context --- Platform
    Context --> State
```

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:91-92](), [CMakeLists.txt:320-371](), [CMakeLists.txt:376-408]()

## Testing the Installation

After building and installing OpenMM, you should verify that it works correctly.

### Running C++ Tests

OpenMM uses CTest for running the C++ test suite:

```bash
# Run all tests
ctest

# Run tests in parallel
ctest --parallel 2

# Run with detailed output
ctest --output-on-failure

# Run specific test
ctest -R TestCudaPlatform
```

**Test Organization:**
- Core tests are in `tests/` directory
- Platform-specific tests in `platforms/*/tests/`
- Plugin tests in `plugins/*/tests/` or `plugins/*/serialization/tests/`

Sources: [devtools/run-ctest.py:1-125](), [CMakeLists.txt:455-469]()

### Running Python Tests

If you built Python wrappers, test them using pytest:

```bash
# Quick installation test
python -m openmm.testInstallation

# Run full Python test suite
cd python/tests
pytest -v
```

**Python Test Files:**
- Unit system tests: `wrappers/python/tests/TestUnits.py`
- Other Python API tests in `wrappers/python/tests/Test*.py`

Sources: [.travis.yml:215-216](), [wrappers/python/tests/TestUnits.py:1-10](), [wrappers/python/tests/pytest.ini:1-2]()

### CI Test Configuration

The OpenMM CI systems run comprehensive tests across platforms:

**Travis CI Test Matrix:**
- CPU with OpenCL on Linux (Ubuntu Xenial)
- CUDA compilation test (no GPU execution)
- macOS with Xcode 9.3
- Static library build
- Multiple Python versions (3.6, 3.8)
- ARM64 and PPC64LE architectures

**Appveyor Test Matrix:**
- Windows with Visual Studio 2019
- OpenCL compilation and testing

**Test Options:**
```bash
# Run with timeout (in seconds)
ctest --timeout 180

# Stop at specific time
ctest --stop-time 12:00:00

# Rerun failed tests only
ctest --rerun-failed
```

Sources: [.travis.yml:16-123](), [appveyor.yml:1-65](), [devtools/run-ctest.py:72-93]()

## Verifying Platform Availability

After installation, check which platforms are available:

```python
from openmm import Platform

# List all available platforms
print(f"Number of platforms: {Platform.getNumPlatforms()}")
for i in range(Platform.getNumPlatforms()):
    platform = Platform.getPlatform(i)
    print(f"Platform {i}: {platform.getName()}")

# Get platform properties
platform = Platform.getPlatformByName('CUDA')
print(f"CUDA version: {platform.getPropertyValue(None, 'CudaCompiler')}")
```

**Expected Platforms Based on Build Configuration:**
- `Reference` - Always available
- `CPU` - If `OPENMM_BUILD_CPU_LIB=ON` and SSE 4.1+ available
- `CUDA` - If CUDA Toolkit found and `OPENMM_BUILD_CUDA_LIB=ON`
- `OpenCL` - If OpenCL SDK found and `OPENMM_BUILD_OPENCL_LIB=ON`
- `HIP` - If ROCm found and `OPENMM_BUILD_HIP_LIB=ON`

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:316-372]()

## Library Installation Structure

OpenMM installs into a structured directory layout:

### Installation Directory Structure

```
/usr/local/openmm/  (or CMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX)
├── lib/
│   ├── libOpenMM.so                    # Core library
│   ├── libOpenMM_static.a              # Static library (if enabled)
│   ├── libOpenMMCPU.so                 # CPU platform
│   ├── libOpenMMCuda.so                # CUDA platform (if built)
│   ├── libOpenMMOpenCL.so              # OpenCL platform (if built)
│   ├── libOpenMMHIP.so                 # HIP platform (if built)
│   └── plugins/
│       ├── libOpenMMAmoebaReference.so  # Amoeba plugin platforms
│       ├── libOpenMMAmoebaCuda.so
│       ├── libOpenMMAmoebaOpenCL.so
│       ├── libOpenMMDrudeReference.so   # Drude plugin platforms
│       ├── libOpenMMRPMDReference.so    # RPMD plugin platforms
│       └── ...
├── include/
│   └── openmm/
│       ├── *.h                          # Public API headers
│       ├── internal/                    # Internal headers
│       ├── reference/                   # Reference platform headers
│       ├── cpu/                         # CPU platform headers
│       └── serialization/               # Serialization headers
└── lib/python3.x/site-packages/
    └── openmm/                          # Python package (if built)
        ├── __init__.py
        ├── app/                         # Application layer
        ├── unit/                        # Unit system
        └── _openmm.so                   # SWIG-generated extension
```

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:410-427](), [plugins/amoeba/CMakeLists.txt:168-177](), [plugins/drude/CMakeLists.txt:151-160](), [plugins/rpmd/CMakeLists.txt:140-152]()

## Common Build Issues and Solutions

### Issue: CMake Cannot Find CUDA

**Symptoms:**
```
CMake Warning: Could not find CUDAToolkit
```

**Solution:**
```bash
# Set CUDA paths explicitly
cmake .. \
  -DCUDA_TOOLKIT_ROOT_DIR=/usr/local/cuda-11.0 \
  -DCUDA_CUDART_LIBRARY=/usr/local/cuda-11.0/lib64/libcudart.so \
  -DCUDA_NVCC_EXECUTABLE=/usr/local/cuda-11.0/bin/nvcc
```

Sources: [.travis.yml:57-62]()

### Issue: Clang 3.6 Compilation Failure

**Symptoms:**
```
CMake Error: The OpenMM CPU platform cannot be built with clang-3.6
```

**Solution:**
Upgrade to clang 3.7+, downgrade to clang 3.5, or switch to GCC. Clang 3.6 has known bugs in AVX support.

Sources: [platforms/cpu/CMakeLists.txt:35-40]()

### Issue: Python Wrappers Require Plugins

**Symptoms:**
```
CMake Error: The Python wrappers require that the AMOEBA/RPMD/Drude plugin be built.
```

**Solution:**
Either enable all three plugins or disable Python wrappers:
```bash
# Enable all plugins (default)
cmake .. -DOPENMM_BUILD_AMOEBA_PLUGIN=ON \
         -DOPENMM_BUILD_RPMD_PLUGIN=ON \
         -DOPENMM_BUILD_DRUDE_PLUGIN=ON

# Or disable Python wrappers
cmake .. -DOPENMM_BUILD_PYTHON_WRAPPERS=OFF
```

Sources: [CMakeLists.txt:439-447]()

### Issue: OpenCL Headers Not Found

**Symptoms:**
```
Could not find OpenCL headers
```

**Solution (Linux/macOS):**
```bash
# Install OpenCL development files
# Ubuntu/Debian:
sudo apt-get install opencl-headers ocl-icd-opencl-dev

# macOS: OpenCL included with Xcode
```

**Solution (Windows):**
Download and build OpenCL ICD loader as shown in Appveyor configuration.

Sources: [appveyor.yml:25-41]()

This page describes the foundational components and architecture that power OpenMM simulations. It explains the high-level design, core API classes, and relationships between key components that make up OpenMM's internal structure. For specific information about how forces are calculated, see [Force Calculation System](#2.2), and for details on time integration, see [Integration System](#2.3).

## Core Components Overview

OpenMM's architecture is built around several key components that work together to define, manage, and execute molecular simulations. These components form a layered structure with a clear separation of concerns.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class System {
        +addParticle()
        +addConstraint()
        +addForce()
        +getDefaultPeriodicBoxVectors()
    }
    
    class Context {
        +getState()
        +setState()
        +getParameters()
        +setParameter()
        +getIntegrator()
    }
    
    class ContextImpl {
        -platformData
        +calcForcesAndEnergy()
        +getForceImpls()
        +applyConstraints()
    }
    
    class State {
        +getPositions()
        +getVelocities()
        +getForces()
        +getEnergy()
        +getParameters()
    }
    
    class Platform {
        +createKernel()
        +supportsKernels()
        +getSpeed()
        +contextCreated()
    }
    
    class KernelImpl {
        <<abstract>>
    }
    
    class Force {
        <<abstract>>
        +createImpl()
        +getForceGroup()
        +usesPeriodicBoundaryConditions()
    }
    
    class ForceImpl {
        <<abstract>>
        +initialize()
        +calcForcesAndEnergy()
        +getKernelNames()
    }
    
    class Integrator {
        <<abstract>>
        +step()
        +getKernelNames()
        +initialize()
    }
    
    Context --> System : references
    Context --> Integrator : references
    Context --> Platform : references
    Context "1" *-- "1" ContextImpl : owns
    ContextImpl --> System : references 
    ContextImpl --> Integrator : references
    ContextImpl --> Platform : uses
    ContextImpl "1" *-- "*" ForceImpl : contains
    System "1" *-- "*" Force : contains
    Force "1" --> "1" ForceImpl : creates
    Platform "1" *-- "*" KernelImpl : provides
    ContextImpl --> KernelImpl : uses
    ContextImpl --> State : produces
```

Sources:
- [openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h]()
- [openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h]()
- [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp]()
- [openmmapi/include/openmm/State.h]()
- [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp]()

The core architecture is organized around these primary components:

1. **System**: Defines the physical model including particles, forces, and constraints
2. **Context**: Main interface for users to interact with the simulation
3. **ContextImpl**: Internal implementation that manages the actual computation
4. **Platform**: Provides hardware-specific implementations of all computation kernels
5. **Kernels**: Individual computational components implementing specific algorithms
6. **Forces**: Components that define interactions between particles
7. **Integrators**: Algorithms for advancing the simulation through time
8. **State**: Container for the current state of the simulation

## Context Lifecycle

The Context is the central object that manages a molecular simulation. It coordinates the interaction between the physical system definition, the integration algorithm, and the hardware platform.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Context
    participant ContextImpl
    participant Platform
    participant Forces
    participant Kernels
    
    User->>Context: create(System, Integrator[, Platform])
    Context->>ContextImpl: construct
    ContextImpl->>Platform: selectPlatform()
    Platform-->>ContextImpl: platform instance
    
    ContextImpl->>Platform: contextCreated()
    Platform-->>ContextImpl: platformData
    
    ContextImpl->>Forces: createImpl() for each Force
    Forces-->>ContextImpl: ForceImpl instances
    
    loop For each required kernel
        ContextImpl->>Platform: createKernel()
        Platform-->>ContextImpl: KernelImpl
    end
    
    ContextImpl->>Kernels: initialize()
    Context->>User: return Context
    
    User->>Context: setPositions()
    Context->>ContextImpl: setPositions()
    ContextImpl->>Kernels: updateStateDataKernel.setPositions()
    
    User->>Context: getState()
    Context->>ContextImpl: calcForcesAndEnergy()
    ContextImpl->>Kernels: initialize forces
    loop For each ForceImpl
        ContextImpl->>Forces: calcForcesAndEnergy()
    end
    ContextImpl->>Kernels: finish calculation
    Kernels-->>ContextImpl: energy
    ContextImpl-->>Context: State information
    Context-->>User: State object
```

Sources:
- [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:43-71]()
- [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:56-164]()
- [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:302-317]()

When a Context is created:

1. The constructor determines which Platform to use, either explicitly specified or chosen automatically based on available hardware and required kernels.
2. It creates a ContextImpl object that will handle the actual computation.
3. The ContextImpl initializes:
   - Creates ForceImpl objects for each Force in the System
   - Creates kernel implementations for all required kernels
   - Sets up initial state (default particle positions, velocities, etc.)
4. Once initialization is complete, the Context can be used to:
   - Set particle positions and velocities
   - Calculate forces and energies
   - Step the simulation forward using the Integrator
   - Retrieve the current State of the simulation

## Kernel-Based Architecture

OpenMM uses a kernel-based architecture to support multiple platforms (CPU, CUDA, OpenCL, etc.) while maintaining a single public API. Each platform provides implementations of various kernels that perform specific computational tasks.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Kernel Hierarchy"
        KernelImpl["KernelImpl (Abstract Base)"]
        
        CalcForcesKernel["CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel"] --> KernelImpl
        UpdateStateKernel["UpdateStateDataKernel"] --> KernelImpl
        ConstraintsKernel["ApplyConstraintsKernel"] --> KernelImpl
        VirtualSitesKernel["VirtualSitesKernel"] --> KernelImpl
        
        ForceKernels["Force-Specific Kernels"] --> KernelImpl
        IntegratorKernels["Integrator Kernels"] --> KernelImpl
    end
    
    subgraph "Platform Implementations"
        CudaKernels["CUDA Kernels"]
        OpenCLKernels["OpenCL Kernels"] 
        ReferenceKernels["Reference Kernels"]
        CPUKernels["CPU Kernels"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Kernel Registry"
        Platform["Platform Class"]
        KernelFactory["KernelFactory Interface"]
        PlatformData["Platform-Specific Data"]
    end
    
    Platform -- KernelFactory
    KernelFactory --> ReferenceKernels
    KernelFactory --> CudaKernels
    KernelFactory --> OpenCLKernels
    KernelFactory --> CPUKernels
    
    CalcForcesKernel -.-> ReferenceKernels
    UpdateStateKernel -.-> ReferenceKernels
    ConstraintsKernel -.-> ReferenceKernels
    
    CalcForcesKernel -.-> CudaKernels
    UpdateStateKernel -.-> CudaKernels
    ConstraintsKernel -.-> CudaKernels
    
    Platform -- PlatformData
```

Sources:
- [olla/include/openmm/kernels.h:83-130]()
- [olla/include/openmm/kernels.h:127-238]()
- [platforms/reference/src/ReferenceKernelFactory.cpp:39-116]()
- [platforms/reference/include/ReferenceKernels.h:78-116]()

Key aspects of the kernel architecture:

1. **Kernel Interface**: Each computational task is defined by a kernel interface, which declares the methods required for that task.

2. **Platform Independence**: The kernel interfaces are platform-independent, allowing the same high-level code to run on any supported hardware.

3. **Core Kernels**: The most important kernels include:
   - `CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel`: Coordinates force calculation and energy summation
   - `UpdateStateDataKernel`: Manages access to state data (positions, velocities, etc.)
   - `ApplyConstraintsKernel`: Implements constraint algorithms
   - `VirtualSitesKernel`: Handles virtual site calculations

4. **Force-Specific Kernels**: Each Force type has one or more corresponding kernels that implement its specific calculations.

5. **Kernel Registration**: Platforms register kernel factories during initialization, which are used to create the appropriate implementation of each required kernel.

## Platform System

Platforms in OpenMM encapsulate hardware-specific implementations of computational kernels. The Platform class serves as a factory for creating kernel implementations tailored to specific hardware.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Platform {
        <<abstract>>
        +getName()
        +getSpeed()
        +supportsDoublePrecision()
        +registerKernelFactory()
        +createKernel()
        +contextCreated()
        +contextDestroyed()
    }
    
    class ReferencePlatform {
        +PlatformData
        +getName(): "Reference" 
        +getSpeed(): 1
        +supportsDoublePrecision(): true
    }
    
    class CPUPlatform {
        +getName(): "CPU"
        +getSpeed(): ~10
    }
    
    class CUDAPlatform {
        +getName(): "CUDA"
        +getSpeed(): ~100
    }
    
    class OpenCLPlatform {
        +getName(): "OpenCL"
        +getSpeed(): ~100
    }
    
    class KernelFactory {
        <<interface>>
        +createKernelImpl()
    }
    
    class ReferenceKernelFactory {
        +createKernelImpl()
    }
    
    class ComputeContext {
        +getForceInfos()
        +createProgram()
        +clearBuffer()
        +getIntegrationUtilities()
    }
    
    Platform <|-- ReferencePlatform
    Platform <|-- CPUPlatform
    Platform <|-- CUDAPlatform
    Platform <|-- OpenCLPlatform
    
    Platform "1" *-- "*" KernelFactory
    KernelFactory <|.. ReferenceKernelFactory
    
    CPUPlatform -- ComputeContext
    CUDAPlatform -- ComputeContext
    OpenCLPlatform -- ComputeContext
```

Sources:
- [platforms/reference/src/ReferencePlatform.cpp:42-81]()
- [platforms/reference/src/ReferenceKernelFactory.cpp:39-116]()
- [platforms/common/include/openmm/common/ComputeContext.h:63-183]()

Key aspects of the platform system:

1. **Platform Base Class**: The abstract `Platform` class defines the interface for platform-specific implementations.

2. **Platform Registry**: OpenMM maintains a registry of available platforms, allowing it to select the appropriate one based on hardware availability and performance.

3. **Platform Selection**: When creating a Context, OpenMM selects a platform either:
   - Explicitly specified by the user
   - Automatically chosen based on available hardware and required kernels
   - Determined by the `OPENMM_DEFAULT_PLATFORM` environment variable

4. **PlatformData**: Each platform implementation creates platform-specific data structures when a context is created, which are used by kernel implementations.

5. **Kernel Creation**: Platforms use registered KernelFactories to create implementations of required kernels.

6. **Reference Platform**: Serves as the reference implementation for all kernels, focusing on correctness rather than performance.

7. **GPU Platforms**: CUDA and OpenCL platforms share much of their implementation through the ComputeContext class, which provides utilities for managing GPU resources.

## State Management

The State object captures a snapshot of the simulation at a point in time. It can include various types of data, such as positions, velocities, forces, and energies.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class State {
        -time: double
        -stepCount: long long
        -positions: vector~Vec3~
        -velocities: vector~Vec3~
        -forces: vector~Vec3~
        -energies: {kinetic, potential}
        -parameters: map~string,double~
        -periodicBoxVectors: Vec3[3]
        -dataTypes: int
        
        +getTime()
        +getStepCount()
        +getPositions()
        +getVelocities()
        +getForces()
        +getKineticEnergy()
        +getPotentialEnergy()
        +getParameters()
        +getPeriodicBoxVectors()
    }
    
    class DataType {
        <<enumeration>>
        Positions
        Velocities
        Forces
        Energy
        Parameters
        ParameterDerivatives
        IntegratorParameters
    }
    
    class StateBuilder {
        +setPositions()
        +setVelocities()
        +setForces()
        +setEnergy()
        +setParameters()
        +setEnergyParameterDerivatives()
        +getState()
    }
    
    class Context {
        +getState()
        +setState()
    }
    
    class UpdateStateDataKernel {
        +getPositions()
        +getVelocities()
        +getForces()
        +getEnergyParameterDerivatives()
        +getTime()
        +getPeriodicBoxVectors()
    }
    
    State -- DataType
    State <|.. StateBuilder : creates
    Context --> State : produces
    Context --> UpdateStateDataKernel : uses
    UpdateStateDataKernel --> State : populates
```

Sources:
- [openmmapi/include/openmm/State.h:55-87]()
- [openmmapi/src/State.cpp:38-84]()
- [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:89-154]()
- [platforms/reference/src/ReferenceKernels.cpp:210-246]()
- [platforms/common/src/CommonKernels.cpp:60-298]()

State management involves:

1. **State Creation**: When Context.getState() is called, the Context uses kernel implementations to gather the requested data (positions, velocities, forces, energies, etc.).

2. **Data Types**: The State.DataType enumeration allows specifying which types of data to include in a State object.

3. **State Builder Pattern**: The StateBuilder class implements a builder pattern to construct State objects with the requested data.

4. **Cross-Platform Support**: Each platform's UpdateStateDataKernel implementation provides methods to get and set state data.

5. **Force Calculation**: When forces or energies are requested, the Context triggers a force calculation using calcForcesAndEnergy().

6. **State Serialization**: State objects can be serialized for checkpoint/restart purposes or for analysis.

## Force Calculation Process

Force calculation is a central part of every molecular simulation. OpenMM uses a modular approach where each Force object has a corresponding ForceImpl that handles the actual calculation.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Context
    participant ContextImpl
    participant CalcForcesKernel
    participant ForceImpl
    participant ForceKernel
    
    Context->>ContextImpl: getState(Forces | Energy)
    ContextImpl->>ContextImpl: calcForcesAndEnergy()
    ContextImpl->>CalcForcesKernel: beginComputation()
    CalcForcesKernel->>CalcForcesKernel: zero forces
    
    loop For each ForceImpl
        ContextImpl->>ForceImpl: calcForcesAndEnergy()
        ForceImpl->>ForceKernel: calculate force
        ForceKernel->>ForceKernel: update force array
        ForceKernel-->>ForceImpl: energy
        ForceImpl-->>ContextImpl: energy
    end
    
    ContextImpl->>CalcForcesKernel: finishComputation()
    CalcForcesKernel->>CalcForcesKernel: validate results
    CalcForcesKernel-->>ContextImpl: energy
    ContextImpl-->>Context: total energy
```

Sources:
- [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:302-317]()
- [platforms/reference/src/ReferenceKernels.cpp:160-185]() 
- [platforms/common/src/CommonKernels.cpp:60-298]()

The force calculation process includes:

1. **Initialization**: The `CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel` initializes the calculation by clearing force arrays.

2. **Force Calculation**: Each `ForceImpl` calculates its contribution to the forces and energy.

3. **Force Types**: OpenMM supports various force types:
   - Bonded forces (bonds, angles, torsions)
   - Nonbonded forces (electrostatics, van der Waals)
   - Custom forces for specialized interactions

4. **Force Groups**: Forces can be organized into groups, allowing selective inclusion in calculations.

5. **Energy Summation**: The total energy is calculated by summing contributions from all active force components.

6. **Multithreading**: Platforms may implement parallel force calculations for better performance.

7. **Cutoffs and Periodic Boundary Conditions**: Platforms handle various optimizations for long-range interactions.

## Integration Process

Integration advances the simulation through time. Different integrators implement various algorithms for numerical integration of the equations of motion.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Integrator Hierarchy"
        Integrator["Integrator (Abstract Base)"]
        Verlet["VerletIntegrator"]
        Langevin["LangevinIntegrator"]
        Brownian["BrownianIntegrator"]
        Custom["CustomIntegrator"]
        
        Integrator --> Verlet
        Integrator --> Langevin
        Integrator --> Brownian
        Integrator --> Custom
    end
    
    subgraph "Integration Process"
        Context["Context"] --> Integrator
        Integrator --> ContextImpl["ContextImpl"]
        ContextImpl --> Kernels["Integration Kernels"]
        Kernels --> Forces["Force Calculation"]
        Kernels --> Constraints["Constraint Application"]
        Forces --> Integration["Time Integration"]
        Constraints --> Integration
        Integration --> VirtualSites["Virtual Site Update"]
        VirtualSites --> StateUpdate["State Update"]
    end
```

Sources:
- [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:302-317]()
- [olla/include/openmm/kernels.h:650-705]()
- [platforms/reference/src/ReferenceKernels.cpp:160-185]()

The integration process includes:

1. **Time Step Execution**: When the Integrator.step() method is called, it delegates to platform-specific kernel implementations.

2. **Force Calculation**: The integrator requests force calculations via ContextImpl.calcForcesAndEnergy().

3. **State Update**: Kernels update positions and velocities according to the integration algorithm.

4. **Constraint Application**: After updating positions, constraints are applied to maintain fixed bond lengths or angles.

5. **Virtual Site Update**: Positions of virtual sites are recalculated based on the new positions of real particles.

6. **Multiple Algorithms**: OpenMM provides several built-in integrators and allows custom algorithm implementation through CustomIntegrator.

## Platform-Specific Implementation Details

While the kernel interfaces are platform-independent, their implementations are specific to each platform. This section highlights the significant differences between platforms.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "Platform Implementation Classes"
        Platform["Platform (Base)"]
        Reference["ReferencePlatform"]
        CPU["CPUPlatform"]
        CUDA["CUDAPlatform"]
        OpenCL["OpenCLPlatform"]
        
        Platform --> Reference
        Platform --> CPU
        Platform --> CUDA
        Platform --> OpenCL
    end
    
    subgraph "Implementation Patterns"
        Reference --> RefKernels["ReferenceKernels"]
        CPU --> CommonKernels["CommonKernels"]
        CUDA --> CommonKernels
        OpenCL --> CommonKernels
        
        RefKernels --> RefPlatformData["ReferencePlatformData"]
        CommonKernels --> ComputeContext["ComputeContext"]
        
        ComputeContext --> ThreadPool["ThreadPool"]
        ComputeContext --> BondedUtilities["BondedUtilities"]
        ComputeContext --> NonbondedUtilities["NonbondedUtilities"]
        ComputeContext --> IntegrationUtilities["IntegrationUtilities"]
    end
```

Sources:
- [platforms/reference/include/ReferencePlatform.h:49-78]()
- [platforms/reference/src/ReferencePlatform.cpp:100-120]()
- [platforms/common/include/openmm/common/ComputeContext.h:63-183]()
- [platforms/common/src/ComputeContext.cpp:47-193]()

Key platform implementation details:

1. **Reference Platform**: 
   - Straightforward C++ implementations focused on correctness
   - No performance optimizations
   - Serves as the gold standard for validating other platforms

2. **GPU Platforms (CUDA and OpenCL)**:
   - Share common code through ComputeContext class
   - Implement specialized kernels for GPU execution
   - Use ComputeProgram and ComputeKernel abstractions to handle platform-specific compilation
   - Employ various optimizations:
     - Specialized data structures for efficient memory access
     - Work division for parallel execution
     - Memory layout optimizations for coalesced access

3. **CPU Platform**:
   - Optimized for multi-core CPU execution
   - Uses SIMD instructions where available
   - Shares some code with GPU platforms via CommonKernels

4. **PlatformData**:
   - Each platform maintains context-specific data
   - Reference platform uses simple C++ data structures
   - GPU platforms maintain device memory buffers and kernel objects

## Conclusion

OpenMM's core architecture is designed to provide a flexible, extensible framework for molecular simulation that can efficiently utilize diverse hardware platforms. The key design principles include:

1. **Separation of Interface and Implementation**: The public API is platform-independent, while implementations are platform-specific.

2. **Modular Design**: Functionality is divided into independent components that can be combined as needed.

3. **Extensibility**: The system can be extended with new forces, integrators, and platforms.

4. **Performance Optimization**: Platform-specific implementations allow for hardware-specific optimizations.

This architecture enables OpenMM to provide both a user-friendly API for application developers and high-performance implementations for computational efficiency.

Sources:
- [openmmapi/include/OpenMM.h:1-87]()
- [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:56-164]()
- [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:43-71]()

## Purpose and Scope

This page describes OpenMM's platform abstraction layer and the kernel pattern that enables runtime selection of optimized implementations for different hardware backends. This architectural pattern allows the same high-level simulation code to execute on CPUs, NVIDIA GPUs (CUDA), AMD GPUs (OpenCL/HIP), or other platforms without modification. 

For information about specific platform implementations and their optimizations, see [Platform Implementations](#3). For details on how forces are calculated across platforms, see [Force Calculation Pipeline](#2.3).

## Core Abstraction Pattern

OpenMM separates the **what** (high-level simulation operations) from the **how** (platform-specific implementations) through a three-layer pattern:

1. **Kernel Interfaces** (`KernelImpl` subclasses) - Define abstract operations like force calculation, state updates, and integration
2. **Platform Classes** - Register and manage available hardware backends (Reference, CPU, CUDA, OpenCL, HIP)
3. **Kernel Factories** - Create platform-specific kernel implementations at runtime

This pattern enables:
- **Hardware portability**: Same API works across all platforms
- **Runtime selection**: Platform chosen when creating a `Context`, not at compile time
- **Extensibility**: New platforms and forces added without modifying core code
- **Performance**: Each platform provides optimized implementations

Sources: [openmmapi/include/openmm/kernels.h:82-125](), [platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernels.h:46-83](), [platforms/opencl/include/OpenCLKernels.h:46-83]()

## Kernel Interface Hierarchy

```mermaid
graph TB
    KernelImpl["KernelImpl<br/>(Abstract Base)"]
    
    subgraph "Core Simulation Kernels"
        CalcForcesKernel["CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/>beginComputation()<br/>finishComputation()"]
        UpdateStateKernel["UpdateStateDataKernel<br/>getPositions()<br/>setPositions()<br/>getForces()"]
        ApplyConstraintsKernel["ApplyConstraintsKernel<br/>apply()<br/>applyToVelocities()"]
        VirtualSitesKernel["VirtualSitesKernel<br/>computePositions()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Force Calculation Kernels"
        HarmonicBondKernel["CalcHarmonicBondForceKernel<br/>initialize()<br/>execute()"]
        NonbondedKernel["CalcNonbondedForceKernel<br/>initialize()<br/>execute()"]
        CustomBondKernel["CalcCustomBondForceKernel"]
        OtherForceKernels["50+ other force kernels..."]
    end
    
    subgraph "Integration Kernels"
        VerletKernel["IntegrateVerletStepKernel<br/>execute()"]
        LangevinKernel["IntegrateLangevinMiddleStepKernel<br/>execute()"]
        CustomIntegratorKernel["IntegrateCustomStepKernel"]
    end
    
    KernelImpl --> CalcForcesKernel
    KernelImpl --> UpdateStateKernel
    KernelImpl --> ApplyConstraintsKernel
    KernelImpl --> VirtualSitesKernel
    KernelImpl --> HarmonicBondKernel
    KernelImpl --> NonbondedKernel
    KernelImpl --> CustomBondKernel
    KernelImpl --> OtherForceKernels
    KernelImpl --> VerletKernel
    KernelImpl --> LangevinKernel
    KernelImpl --> CustomIntegratorKernel
```

**Key Kernel Categories**

| Kernel Type | Purpose | Key Methods | Examples |
|------------|---------|-------------|----------|
| **Core Simulation** | Orchestrate force/energy computation lifecycle | `beginComputation()`, `finishComputation()` | `CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel` |
| **State Management** | Get/set particle positions, velocities, forces | `getPositions()`, `setVelocities()`, `getForces()` | `UpdateStateDataKernel` |
| **Force Calculation** | Compute forces and energies for specific force types | `initialize()`, `execute()` | `CalcNonbondedForceKernel`, `CalcHarmonicBondForceKernel` |
| **Integration** | Advance simulation time by updating positions/velocities | `execute()`, `computeKineticEnergy()` | `IntegrateVerletStepKernel` |
| **Constraints** | Apply distance constraints (SHAKE/SETTLE) | `apply()`, `applyToVelocities()` | `ApplyConstraintsKernel` |

Each kernel interface is an abstract class defining pure virtual methods. Platform-specific implementations override these methods with optimized code.

Sources: [openmmapi/include/openmm/kernels.h:87-1068](), [platforms/reference/include/ReferenceKernels.h:73-115]()

## Platform-Specific Implementations

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Abstract Kernel Interface"
        AbstractKernel["CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/><br/>+ initialize(System)<br/>+ beginComputation(...)<br/>+ finishComputation(...)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Reference Platform"
        RefKernel["ReferenceCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/><br/>Single-threaded C++<br/>Simple, readable code<br/>Correctness baseline"]
    end
    
    subgraph "CPU Platform"
        CpuKernel["CommonCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/>via CommonKernels.h<br/><br/>Multi-threaded<br/>SSE/AVX SIMD<br/>Cache-friendly"]
    end
    
    subgraph "CUDA Platform"
        CudaKernel["CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/><br/>CUDA kernels<br/>GPU optimized<br/>High performance"]
    end
    
    subgraph "OpenCL Platform"
        OpenCLKernel["OpenCLCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/><br/>OpenCL kernels<br/>Cross-vendor GPUs<br/>Portable"]
    end
    
    AbstractKernel -.->|implements| RefKernel
    AbstractKernel -.->|implements| CpuKernel
    AbstractKernel -.->|implements| CudaKernel
    AbstractKernel -.->|implements| OpenCLKernel
```

**Implementation Characteristics by Platform**

| Platform | Kernel Implementation Base | Context Type | Typical Speedup | Use Case |
|----------|---------------------------|--------------|-----------------|----------|
| **Reference** | `ReferenceCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel` | N/A (CPU only) | 1x (baseline) | Debugging, validation |
| **CPU** | `CommonKernels.h` (shared with GPU) | `ComputeContext` | 4-8x | Multi-core CPUs |
| **CUDA** | `CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel` | `CudaContext` | 50-200x | NVIDIA GPUs |
| **OpenCL** | `OpenCLCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel` | `OpenCLContext` | 40-150x | AMD/Intel GPUs |

Each platform implementation:
- Inherits from the abstract kernel interface
- Receives a platform-specific context (`CudaContext`, `OpenCLContext`, etc.) that provides hardware access
- Implements the same virtual methods with platform-optimized code

Sources: [platforms/reference/include/ReferenceKernels.h:78-115](), [platforms/cuda/include/CudaKernels.h:46-83](), [platforms/opencl/include/OpenCLKernels.h:46-83](), [platforms/common/include/openmm/common/CommonKernels.h:46-160]()

## Platform and KernelFactory Architecture

```mermaid
graph TB
    Platform["Platform<br/>(Abstract Base Class)<br/><br/>+ getName()<br/>+ getSpeed()<br/>+ createKernel(name, context)"]
    
    subgraph "Platform Implementations"
        RefPlatform["ReferencePlatform<br/><br/>Speed: 1.0<br/>Always available"]
        CudaPlatform["CudaPlatform<br/><br/>Speed: 100.0<br/>Requires CUDA SDK"]
        OpenCLPlatform["OpenCLPlatform<br/><br/>Speed: 50.0<br/>Requires OpenCL"]
    end
    
    Platform --> RefPlatform
    Platform --> CudaPlatform
    Platform --> OpenCLPlatform
    
    KernelFactory["KernelFactory<br/>(Abstract)<br/><br/>+ createKernelImpl(name, platform, context)"]
    
    subgraph "Factory Implementations"
        RefFactory["ReferenceKernelFactory<br/><br/>Creates Reference kernels"]
        CudaFactory["CudaKernelFactory<br/><br/>Creates CUDA kernels"]
        OpenCLFactory["OpenCLKernelFactory<br/><br/>Creates OpenCL kernels"]
    end
    
    KernelFactory --> RefFactory
    KernelFactory --> CudaFactory
    KernelFactory --> OpenCLFactory
    
    RefPlatform -->|registers| RefFactory
    CudaPlatform -->|registers| CudaFactory
    OpenCLPlatform -->|registers| OpenCLFactory
    
    RefFactory -.->|"creates<br/>ReferenceCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/>ReferenceUpdateStateDataKernel<br/>etc."| RefKernels["Reference Kernels"]
    CudaFactory -.->|"creates<br/>CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/>CommonUpdateStateDataKernel<br/>etc."| CudaKernels["CUDA Kernels"]
    OpenCLFactory -.->|"creates<br/>OpenCLCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/>CommonUpdateStateDataKernel<br/>etc."| OpenCLKernels["OpenCL Kernels"]
```

**Platform Registration Process**

Each platform implementation follows this pattern:

1. **Constructor creates KernelFactory** and registers it for each kernel type
2. **Platform registered** with global `Platform` registry at startup
3. **Runtime selection** occurs when user creates a `Context`

Example from CUDA platform:

```cpp
// In CudaPlatform constructor (CudaPlatform.cpp:62-114)
CudaKernelFactory* factory = new CudaKernelFactory();
registerKernelFactory(CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel::Name(), factory);
registerKernelFactory(UpdateStateDataKernel::Name(), factory);
registerKernelFactory(CalcNonbondedForceKernel::Name(), factory);
// ... 40+ more kernel types
```

Sources: [platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp:62-114](), [platforms/opencl/src/OpenCLPlatform.cpp:56-119](), [platforms/reference/src/ReferencePlatform.cpp:41-86]()

## Kernel Creation Flow

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as "User Code"
    participant Platform as "Platform"
    participant ContextImpl as "ContextImpl"
    participant KernelFactory as "KernelFactory"
    participant Kernel as "Platform Kernel"
    
    User->>Platform: selectPlatform("CUDA")
    User->>Platform: createContext(system, integrator)
    Platform->>ContextImpl: new ContextImpl(...)
    
    Note over ContextImpl: For each Force in System
    ContextImpl->>Platform: createKernel(kernelName, context)
    Platform->>Platform: lookup KernelFactory for kernelName
    Platform->>KernelFactory: createKernelImpl(name, platform, context)
    
    alt CUDA Platform
        KernelFactory->>Kernel: new CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel(name, platform, cu)
    else OpenCL Platform
        KernelFactory->>Kernel: new OpenCLCalcNonbondedForceKernel(name, platform, cl)
    else Reference Platform
        KernelFactory->>Kernel: new ReferenceCalcNonbondedForceKernel(name, platform)
    end
    
    KernelFactory-->>Platform: return KernelImpl*
    Platform-->>ContextImpl: return Kernel
    ContextImpl->>Kernel: initialize(system, force)
    
    Note over ContextImpl: Kernels ready for simulation
```

**Kernel Factory Implementation Pattern**

The factory uses string-based kernel names to determine which implementation to create:

```cpp
// From CudaKernelFactory::createKernelImpl (CudaKernelFactory.cpp:43-140)
KernelImpl* CudaKernelFactory::createKernelImpl(std::string name, 
                                                 const Platform& platform, 
                                                 ContextImpl& context) const {
    CudaPlatform::PlatformData& data = *static_cast<CudaPlatform::PlatformData*>(context.getPlatformData());
    CudaContext& cu = *data.contexts[0];
    
    if (name == CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel::Name())
        return new CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel(name, platform, cu);
    if (name == UpdateStateDataKernel::Name())
        return new CommonUpdateStateDataKernel(name, platform, cu);
    if (name == CalcNonbondedForceKernel::Name())
        return new CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel(name, platform, cu, context.getSystem());
    // ... more kernel types
}
```

Note that some kernels (like `UpdateStateDataKernel`) use shared implementations from `CommonKernels.h` that work across GPU platforms.

Sources: [platforms/cuda/src/CudaKernelFactory.cpp:43-140](), [platforms/opencl/src/OpenCLKernelFactory.cpp:41-154](), [platforms/reference/src/ReferenceKernelFactory.cpp:37-148]()

## Runtime Kernel Execution Example

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "User API Layer"
        UserCode["simulation.step(1000)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Context Layer"
        ContextStep["Context.step()"]
        ContextImpl["ContextImpl"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Kernel Orchestration"
        CalcForcesKernel["CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel<br/>(platform-specific)"]
        BeginComp["beginComputation()"]
        ForceKernels["Force Kernels<br/>CalcNonbondedForceKernel<br/>CalcHarmonicBondForceKernel<br/>etc."]
        FinishComp["finishComputation()"]
        IntegratorKernel["IntegrateVerletStepKernel<br/>(platform-specific)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Platform Execution (Example: CUDA)"
        CudaContext["CudaContext"]
        ClearBuffers["clearAutoclearBuffers()"]
        PrepareInteractions["prepareInteractions()"]
        ComputeNonbonded["computeInteractions()<br/>Launch CUDA kernels"]
        ReduceForces["reduceForces()<br/>Sum force contributions"]
        IntegrateCUDA["CUDA integration kernel<br/>Update positions/velocities"]
    end
    
    UserCode --> ContextStep
    ContextStep --> ContextImpl
    ContextImpl --> CalcForcesKernel
    CalcForcesKernel --> BeginComp
    BeginComp --> ClearBuffers
    BeginComp --> PrepareInteractions
    
    PrepareInteractions --> ForceKernels
    ForceKernels --> ComputeNonbonded
    
    ComputeNonbonded --> FinishComp
    FinishComp --> ReduceForces
    
    ReduceForces --> IntegratorKernel
    IntegratorKernel --> IntegrateCUDA
```

**Execution Flow Details**

1. **beginComputation()** ([platforms/cuda/src/CudaKernels.cpp:63-76]())
   - Clears force buffers
   - Updates global parameters
   - Prepares neighbor lists for nonbonded calculations
   - Initializes energy parameter derivative workspace

2. **Force Kernel Execution** (platform-specific)
   - Each `Force` in the `System` has a corresponding kernel
   - Kernels compute forces and add them to force buffers
   - Energy contributions accumulated

3. **finishComputation()** ([platforms/cuda/src/CudaKernels.cpp:78-91]())
   - Executes bonded force computations
   - Executes nonbonded force computations  
   - Reduces forces from multiple buffers
   - Distributes forces to virtual sites
   - Returns total potential energy

4. **Integration**
   - Integrator kernel updates positions and velocities
   - Platform-specific implementation (CUDA, OpenCL, Reference)

Sources: [platforms/cuda/src/CudaKernels.cpp:60-91](), [platforms/opencl/src/OpenCLKernels.cpp:57-87](), [platforms/reference/src/ReferenceKernels.cpp:170-192]()

## Multi-Platform Support for Parallel Execution

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Single GPU Execution"
        SingleFactory["CudaKernelFactory"]
        SingleKernel["CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel"]
        SingleContext["CudaContext (GPU 0)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Multi-GPU Execution"
        ParallelFactory["CudaKernelFactory<br/>(detects multiple contexts)"]
        ParallelKernel["CudaParallelCalcNonbondedForceKernel<br/>(wraps multiple kernels)"]
        Context0["CudaContext (GPU 0)"]
        Context1["CudaContext (GPU 1)"]
        Kernel0["CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel<br/>(GPU 0)"]
        Kernel1["CudaCalcNonbondedForceKernel<br/>(GPU 1)"]
    end
    
    SingleFactory -->|"data.contexts.size() == 1"| SingleKernel
    SingleKernel --> SingleContext
    
    ParallelFactory -->|"data.contexts.size() > 1"| ParallelKernel
    ParallelKernel --> Kernel0
    ParallelKernel --> Kernel1
    Kernel0 --> Context0
    Kernel1 --> Context1
```

**Parallel Kernel Pattern**

When multiple devices are available, the kernel factory creates **parallel wrapper kernels** that coordinate work across devices:

```cpp
// From CudaKernelFactory.cpp:46-66
if (data.contexts.size() > 1) {
    // Multi-device parallel execution
    if (name == CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel::Name())
        return new CudaParallelCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel(name, platform, data);
    if (name == CalcNonbondedForceKernel::Name())
        return new CudaParallelCalcNonbondedForceKernel(name, platform, data, context.getSystem());
    // ...
}
// Single device execution
if (name == CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel::Name())
    return new CudaCalcForcesAndEnergyKernel(name, platform, cu);
```

The parallel kernel:
- Divides particles across GPUs
- Executes force calculations on each GPU in parallel
- Reduces results from all GPUs to compute total energy
- Handles inter-GPU communication for particles near device boundaries

Sources: [platforms/cuda/src/CudaKernelFactory.cpp:43-75](), [platforms/opencl/src/OpenCLKernelFactory.cpp:41-75]()

## Platform Data and Context Management

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Platform Layer"
        Platform["Platform"]
        PlatformData["PlatformData<br/>(platform-specific state)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "CUDA Platform Example"
        CudaPlatformData["CudaPlatform::PlatformData"]
        CudaContexts["vector&lt;CudaContext*&gt; contexts"]
        CudaContext0["CudaContext (device 0)<br/><br/>CUcontext context<br/>CUdevice device<br/>posq, velm, force arrays<br/>BondedUtilities<br/>NonbondedUtilities<br/>IntegrationUtilities"]
        CudaContext1["CudaContext (device 1)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "OpenCL Platform Example"
        OpenCLPlatformData["OpenCLPlatform::PlatformData"]
        OpenCLContexts["vector&lt;OpenCLContext*&gt; contexts"]
        OpenCLContext0["OpenCLContext (device 0)<br/><br/>cl::Context context<br/>cl::Device device<br/>posq, velm, force arrays<br/>BondedUtilities<br/>NonbondedUtilities<br/>IntegrationUtilities"]
    end
    
    Platform --> PlatformData
    PlatformData -.->|"CUDA"| CudaPlatformData
    PlatformData -.->|"OpenCL"| OpenCLPlatformData
    
    CudaPlatformData --> CudaContexts
    CudaContexts --> CudaContext0
    CudaContexts --> CudaContext1
    
    OpenCLPlatformData --> OpenCLContexts
    OpenCLContexts --> OpenCLContext0
```

**Platform Data Responsibilities**

Each platform maintains a `PlatformData` structure that:

1. **Stores device contexts** - One or more hardware contexts (GPU devices)
2. **Tracks global state** - Time, step count, simulation parameters
3. **Manages resources** - Memory buffers, compiled kernels, thread pools
4. **Coordinates devices** - For multi-GPU execution

The platform-specific context (e.g., `CudaContext`) provides:
- Hardware access (CUDA streams, OpenCL command queues)
- Memory management (device buffers for positions, velocities, forces)
- Utility objects (`BondedUtilities`, `NonbondedUtilities`, `IntegrationUtilities`)
- Kernel compilation and caching

Sources: [platforms/cuda/include/CudaContext.h:86-400](), [platforms/opencl/include/OpenCLContext.h:86-350](), [platforms/cuda/src/CudaPlatform.cpp:217-280](), [platforms/opencl/src/OpenCLPlatform.cpp:224-281]()

## Benefits of the Kernel Pattern

**Separation of Concerns**
- High-level simulation logic (forces, integrators) independent of hardware
- Platform maintainers optimize kernels without changing simulation APIs
- New forces added once, automatically available on all platforms

**Runtime Flexibility**
- Platform selection at `Context` creation, not compile time
- Same executable runs on any available hardware
- Automatic fallback to CPU if GPU unavailable

**Performance Optimization**
- Each platform uses hardware-specific optimizations (SIMD, GPU parallelism)
- Kernel specialization for different precision modes (single, mixed, double)
- Multi-device parallelization handled transparently

**Extensibility**
- Plugin system uses same kernel pattern (see [Plugin System and Extensions](#5))
- Custom platforms can be added without modifying core code
- New kernel types registered dynamically

Sources: [openmmapi/include/openmm/kernels.h:82-125](), [platforms/common/include/openmm/common/ComputeContext.h:1-800]()

# Page: Context and State Management

# Context and State Management

<details>

This document describes the core classes responsible for managing simulation state in OpenMM: `Context` and `State`. These classes form the central interface for controlling molecular simulations, storing simulation data, and capturing system snapshots.

## Overview

The Context and State management system handles:
- Creating and configuring simulation environments
- Storing and retrieving simulation data (positions, velocities, forces, etc.)
- Capturing snapshots of simulation state
- Serializing and deserializing simulation state for checkpointing
- Providing a hardware-agnostic interface for simulation control

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Context {
        +getState()
        +setState()
        +setPositions()
        +setVelocities()
        +getParameter()/setParameter()
        +createCheckpoint()/loadCheckpoint()
        +reinitialize()
    }
    
    class ContextImpl {
        -platformData
        -forceImpls
        -initializeForcesKernel
        -updateStateDataKernel
        -applyConstraintsKernel
        -virtualSitesKernel
        +calcForcesAndEnergy()
        +updateContextState()
    }
    
    class State {
        +getPositions()
        +getVelocities()
        +getForces()
        +getParameters()
        +getEnergy()
        +getTime()
    }
    
    class StateBuilder {
        +setPositions()
        +setVelocities()
        +setForces()
        +setParameters()
        +setEnergy()
        +getState()
    }
    
    Context *-- ContextImpl : owns
    Context --> State : creates
    State *-- StateBuilder : built by
    ContextImpl --> Platform : uses
    ContextImpl --> System : references
    ContextImpl --> Integrator : references
```

Sources: [openmmapi/include/openmm/Context.h:1-302](), [openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h:1-317](), [openmmapi/include/openmm/State.h:1-179]()

## Context Class

The `Context` class is the primary interface for controlling a simulation in OpenMM. It brings together a `System` (which defines particles, forces, and constraints), an `Integrator` (which defines how to advance the simulation in time), and a `Platform` (which handles the computational implementation).

### Creating a Context

A Context can be created in several ways:

```cpp
// Create a Context using the fastest available platform
Context context(system, integrator);

// Create a Context using a specific platform
Context context(system, integrator, platform);

// Create a Context with platform-specific properties
Context context(system, integrator, platform, properties);
```

When creating a Context without specifying a platform, OpenMM selects the fastest available platform that supports all required kernels. The construction process includes validation of the system configuration, initialization of all forces, and preparation of the computational kernels.

Sources: [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:43-65](), [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:56-164]()

### Context State Management

The Context maintains the complete state of a simulation, including:

1. **Time tracking**: Current simulation time and step count
2. **Particle state**: Positions, velocities, and forces
3. **System configuration**: Periodic box vectors and parameters
4. **Energy**: Kinetic and potential energy

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "Context State Management"
        State1["Initial State"] --> Context
        Context --> A["Get/Set Positions"]
        Context --> B["Get/Set Velocities"]
        Context --> C["Get/Set Parameters"]
        Context --> D["Get/Set Time & Step Count"]
        Context --> E["Set Periodic Box Vectors"]
        Context --> F["Apply Constraints"]
        Context --> G["Compute Virtual Sites"]
        
        A --> State2["Updated State"]
        B --> State2
        C --> State2
        D --> State2
        E --> State2
        F --> State2
        G --> State2
        
        Context --> |"getState()"| State3["State Snapshot"]
        State3 --> |"setState()"| Context
    end
```

Sources: [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:89-154](), [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:173-246](), [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:212-300]()

### The State Object

The `State` class captures a snapshot of a simulation at a specific point in time. When creating a State through `Context::getState()`, you specify which data types to include:

```cpp
// Get a State containing positions and velocities
State state = context.getState(State::Positions | State::Velocities);

// Get a complete State with all data
State state = context.getState(State::Positions | State::Velocities | 
                              State::Forces | State::Energy | 
                              State::Parameters | State::ParameterDerivatives |
                              State::IntegratorParameters);
```

The State object provides methods to access the requested data:

```cpp
// Access data from a State object
double time = state.getTime();
long long stepCount = state.getStepCount();
const vector<Vec3>& positions = state.getPositions();
const vector<Vec3>& velocities = state.getVelocities();
const vector<Vec3>& forces = state.getForces();
double kineticEnergy = state.getKineticEnergy();
double potentialEnergy = state.getPotentialEnergy();
const map<string, double>& parameters = state.getParameters();
```

Attempting to access data that wasn't included when creating the State will throw an exception.

Sources: [openmmapi/include/openmm/State.h:44-153](), [openmmapi/src/State.cpp:38-133]()

## Internal Implementation

### ContextImpl

The `ContextImpl` class is the internal implementation of `Context`. It handles the actual work of:
- Managing the computational kernels
- Storing simulation data
- Interacting with the Platform

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class ContextImpl {
        -System system
        -Integrator integrator
        -Platform platform
        -vector<ForceImpl*> forceImpls
        -map<string, double> parameters
        -bool hasInitializedForces
        -bool hasSetPositions
        -Kernel initializeForcesKernel
        -Kernel updateStateDataKernel
        -Kernel applyConstraintsKernel
        -Kernel virtualSitesKernel
        -void* platformData
        +calcForcesAndEnergy()
        +getPositions()/setPositions()
        +getVelocities()/setVelocities()
        +getParameter()/setParameter()
        +createCheckpoint()/loadCheckpoint()
    }
    
    class ForceImpl {
        +updateContextState()
        +calcForcesAndEnergy()
        +getBondedParticles()
    }
    
    ContextImpl "1" *-- "*" ForceImpl : contains
    ContextImpl --> System : references
    ContextImpl --> Integrator : references
    ContextImpl --> Platform : uses
```

A key feature of `ContextImpl` is its ability to interact with various platform implementations through a kernel-based approach. The four essential kernels are:

1. `initializeForcesKernel`: Calculates forces and energy
2. `updateStateDataKernel`: Gets/sets positions, velocities, and other state data
3. `applyConstraintsKernel`: Enforces distance constraints
4. `virtualSitesKernel`: Updates positions of virtual sites

Sources: [openmmapi/include/openmm/internal/ContextImpl.h:53-312](), [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:167-191](), [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:228-356]()

### Force Calculation

The `ContextImpl::calcForcesAndEnergy()` method is responsible for calculating forces and energy. It:

1. Begins force computation through the `CalcForcesAndEnergyKernel`
2. Calls `calcForcesAndEnergy()` on each `ForceImpl` to add their contributions
3. Finishes computation and returns the total energy

This method also allows for selective force group calculation through the `groups` parameter, enabling partial energy evaluations.

Sources: [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:302-317]()

## Checkpointing and Serialization

OpenMM provides two mechanisms for saving and restoring simulation state:

1. **State-based method**: Using `setState()` and `getState()`
2. **Checkpoint-based method**: Using `createCheckpoint()` and `loadCheckpoint()`

The State-based method is more portable but less complete, while the checkpoint method is platform-specific but preserves the internal state more completely.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    subgraph "State-Based Serialization"
        Context1["Context"] --> |"getState()"| State
        State --> |"serialize()"| SerializedState["Serialized State"]
        SerializedState --> |"deserialize()"| ReconstructedState["Reconstructed State"]
        ReconstructedState --> |"setState()"| Context2["New Context"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Checkpoint-Based Serialization"
        ContextA["Context"] --> |"createCheckpoint()"| Checkpoint
        Checkpoint --> |"loadCheckpoint()"| ContextB["Same/New Context"]
    end
```

The checkpointing mechanism writes a complete binary representation of the simulation state, including internal platform data. This allows for exact continuation of a simulation, even preserving the state of random number generators.

Sources: [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:458-503](), [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:257-272](), [serialization/src/StateProxy.cpp:41-159]()

## Context Reinitialization

The `Context::reinitialize()` method allows updating a Context to reflect changes made to the System:

```cpp
// Update the Context after modifying the System
context.reinitialize();

// Preserve the current state during reinitialization
context.reinitialize(true);
```

This is an expensive operation that rebuilds the internal representation of the System. When possible, it's preferable to use the `updateParametersInContext()` method provided by most Force classes for more efficient updates.

Sources: [openmmapi/src/Context.cpp:248-264]()

## Finding Molecular Structure

The Context provides a method to identify the molecular structure of the system:

```cpp
// Get a list of particles in each molecule
const vector<vector<int>>& molecules = context.getMolecules();
```

This method identifies molecules by looking at bonds, constraints, and virtual sites. Particles connected by any of these interactions are considered part of the same molecule.

Sources: [openmmapi/src/ContextImpl.cpp:358-442]()

## Related Concepts

- For details on how forces are calculated within a Context, see [Force Calculation System](#2.2)
- For information about time integration in OpenMM, see [Integration System](#2.3)
- For platform-specific implementations, see [Platform Implementations](#3)

---
